maintopic: STATEMENT IN DEBATE ON DEFENCE ESTIMATES RESPECTING ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
We from the maritimes are particularly interested in this item, having to do with the Royal Canadian Navy.
The question of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) as to submarines or destroyers is one in which I have taken a great deal of interest, and I think the attitude taken by the minister in favour of destroyers is a wise one. In the last war we had a patrol of 123 ships on the Atlantic coast, and we had 21 vessels sunk by submarines off that coast. As I said last year, enemy submarines came within twenty-five miles of the coast of Nova Scotia. I happen to represent a constituency where enemy submarines came within sight of the shore. If that should happen in the next war, we naturally want to be prepared to defend ourselves.
At the outbreak of the last war enemy raiders were at large in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. There was the Karlsruhe and the Crown Prince Wilhelm in the Atlantic, and Von Spee's squadron in the Pacific, which was annihilated with the destruction of the Emden in the Indian ocean. In any event enemy raiders were at large off our Atlantic and Pacific coasts at the outbreak of the last war, and I have no doubt that the same situation would be repeated in another war, but in more intense form.
We should consider this vote very carefully. To enable the committee to appreciate the menace of enemy submarines I will give the dates when they appeared off our Atlantic coast in the last war. The first one appeared in October, 1916; the next on June 2, 1918;

Supply-National Defence
another appeared on August 3, 1918, and enemy submarines were also sighted in various places off the Atlantic coast in the months of October and November, 1918. I am giving a list of places on the Atlantic where the submarines were seen, in order of their last appearance.
I do not mean that these are the only places where they appeared, because prior to this they were seen in a large number of places.
I am trying to make the point that they appeared generally on the Atlantic coast, and not at just one place, and in the next war that we may expect that, shortly after they have appeared at one point they will appeal two or three hundred miles away.
Here is the order of their last appearances. We found them 25 miles west-northwest of Brier island, off the western portion of Nova Scotia; then off Shelburne; then off Halifax; then off Yarmouth; then off Canso; then off St. Pierre-Miquelon, and lastly, off St. Johns, Newfoundland, and that was on November 6, 1918, or just five days before the war ended.
In addition to this menace, German mines were laid on the Atlantic coast. I believe one of those mines was picked up and is in the department here. So that we may expect, in view of what happened in the last war, that from the sea we shall be menaced from various directions: first, from raiders; second, from submarines; third, mines undoubtedly will be laid here and there. That is what happened in the last war. When the war broke out we had no suitable patrol vessels. We started a patrol from Halifax to Sydney and Cape Race, Newfoundland. The patrol from Sydney to Cape Race was largely to cover the gulf of St. Lawrence and protect the traffic coming in through the St. Lawrence river. The submarine patrol started in 1917, and an air patrol was initiated in 1918. When it was necessary to start the air patrol from Sydney and Halifax we had to borrow from the United States the aeroplanes as well as the rest of the necessary equipment to form the patrol. A great part of our merchant marine was not suitably equipped to encounter an enemy, but was good for patrol work only; consequently the development of the patrol work was done largely with British and naval vessels. We had to depend almost entirely on their naval equipment, and when it came to our air patrol we had to rely entirely on the United States. That is a situation which I for one hope will not recur if another war breaks out. I realize of course that important expenditures are being made and I approve heartily of votes of this kind.
The hon. member for Vancouver North suggested that he rather preferred submarines to destroyers. I do not agree with him. I
think we should develop especially our destroyer fleet. The other day the minister said that the plans were to have a flotilla of, I think, eight destroyers and one leader. A destroyer has a speed of something like 35 knots an hour. I assume that the raiders which will have to be looked after will be for the most part merchant vessels having speeds of 20 to 25 knots an hour, and we should be equipped with vessels which are not too expensive-which are within our financial abilities-to look after an- enemy of that kind. Each of the destroyers we now have cost, I believe, about one and a half million dollars. I realize it is almost impossible for us to finance and maintain cruisers whose first cost is about ten million dollars apiece, so that I favour the idea of developing, at least upon the Atlantic coast, a destroyer flotilla with the auxiliary equipment necessary for a reasonable scheme of defence. I hope the department will not take too long in putting these nine destroyers on the Atlantic coast.
It is also important to remember that it takes some time to train men for the naval service. You can train men for the air force in from six to eight months. Men for the army can be trained in from six months to a year. But a man required to serve in the navy must train from four to six years in order that he may be brought up to the recognized standard. I suggest therefore to the department that we should not wait too long before we develop the naval arm.
Speaking the other day of the defence of the Atlantic coast, the minister indicated that the policy of the department was to develop a major naval base at Halifax and an auxiliary one at Sydney. I wish to draw attention to the extent of the traffic and trade which can thus be protected, and to which most damage was done in the last war: it is the traffic which goes from the bay of Fundy and along the southeastern end of Nova Scotia. Allow me briefly to define the courses taken by this traffic. First, you have the general coastal traffic along the shore; second, you have the trade routes between Saint John, New Brunswick and the West Indies, Bermuda, South America and Europe; then you have the trade routes from Halifax to the same places; also there is the traffic from the south going up the St. Lawrence; lastly, the traffic from Nova Scotia to New England. Keeping these in mind, I believe that in the near future the department should seriously consider developing some auxiliary naval base near the southeastern end of the province, on account of the traffic which I have indicated and the damage which was done in the last war.
Supply-National Dejence

I am not suggesting that we should take anything from the other naval bases, nor do I think we should depend entirely on Halifax or Sydney. Other precautions should be developed, and in that connection, places along the western end of Nova Scotia should be investigated seriously. That coast has several harbours which I believe would make ideal protection for a fleet of any size, whether ours or any other. I have in mind more than one location, but I should like to draw attention particularly to the harbour of Shelburne. We have there a stretch of water ideally located, protected from all winds, reasonable of approach, some seven or eight miles in length, with an average width of one to one and a half miles and an average depth of between thirty-five and forty feet-I believe the average is from six to seven fathoms. I suggest to the department that they keep this in mind in a long-range view of naval defence.
I commend heartily the course of the department in developing a fishermen's naval reserve. I hope they will not wait too long, and that steps will be taken this summer to carry into effect the statements made by the minister in his opening speech on the defence estimates. I understand that the thought is to have forty boats and 200 fishermen, to be developed into a fishermen's naval reserve. That could be increased materially, and we have on the coast men who would be very valuable in that they have an intimate knowledge of the coast line.
I would stress, therefore, two points particularly : first, the necessity of providing for naval defence along the southeastern coast of Nova Scotia, and, second, the establishment of a fishermen's naval reserve, numerically as large as possible.

maintopic: STATEMENT IN DEBATE ON DEFENCE ESTIMATES RESPECTING ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
Some points have escaped the attention of the hon. member. We have already six destroyers and are about to procure a flotilla leader. The destroyers will no doubt play a useful part in any scheme of coastal defence, but we are discussing now a long-range program and trends of policy that may develop, and I am anxious to see more adequate provision for the very problem the hon. gentleman has outlined. Additional destroyers cannot be obtained in this country but can be obtained in the United Kingdom. The British navy is developing a type of patrol vessel which can be built in Canada, and that is important because it is becoming increasingly difficult for the United Kingdom to supply our requirements in this regard. A destroyer does not carry guns of sufficient calibre to meet any cruiser that might attack the Canadian shore. The destroyer would have to get out of the way unless by means

of torpedo action it could impede a raiding force. Even armed merchantmen may carry guns of larger calibre than those carried by destroyers. But with the construction in Canada of fast patrol vessels, which are less expensive but still fast enough for the work, a number of these boats could be provided for every destroyer that could be secured, and they could be equipped with modern detection devices and could certainly cover the area of our coast much more efficiently than could any destroyer.
Furthermore, for convoy work, ships coming in close proximity to our harbour's, destroyers travelling at the rate of thirty-five knots an hour are altogether too fast. Slower convoy vessels carrying heavier guns would be more efficient. The minister says that in this regard he is in the hands of the staff. I understand the defence council reported to the defence committee of the cabinet. The minister is the political head of the department and is responsible to parliament, and I do not like to hear the statement from him that the staff alone is determining policy in this matter. We know very well that the majority of the staff have been trained with the British Admiralty, and quite properly so perhaps; but they have learned to accept the British tradition and they believe that their only operations will be in cooperation with the British fleet. In recent years, however, the situation has changed, particularly by reason of the fact that potential enemies have found it possible to establish naval bases from which more effectively to raid British shipping.
The British navy can no longer shield this dominion but will have to fall back more definitely upon the protection of focal areas and ports in the United Kingdom. We have therefore a greater responsibility than ever before, and I urge that our naval defence should be more strictly along Canadian lines and that in some respects we should break with the British tradition. At the outbreak of the last war the commanders of some of our ships held that they should remain at their stations and guard Canadian shipping, but by virtue of the Naval Service Act and orders communicated by the British Admiralty they were sent to sea to engage ships which far outranged them in speed and gun calibre.
I am suggesting not lack of defence or inefficient defence, but that form of naval defence which more adequately meets Canadian needs; and instead of additional destroyers, which could be procured from Great Britain only with great difficulty, I submit that the money could be more effectively spent on patrol vessels carrying torpedo firing equipment, depth charges and detector devices,

Supply-National Defence
vessels capable of operating over a more extensive defence patrol than would be possible with cruisers. In view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Pottier) I suggest that the emphasis should be placed more definitely upon smaller and faster patrol vessels.

maintopic: STATEMENT IN DEBATE ON DEFENCE ESTIMATES RESPECTING ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
I understood the minister to say that in the event of war sufficient cargo tonnage was available. We can all remember that in the last war there was a scarcity of cargo tonnage of all types. At present there is no doubt a large amount of tonnage tied up; a great many boats that were in service during the last war have been scrapped, while the remaining boats are over twenty years old. It is a question therefore whether it would be worth while putting them into service again. May I offer a proposal whereby the government can acquire suitable boats for the defence of our coasts, and that at no cost to the government. I am thinking of boats 260 feet long by 30 feet in breadth and 12J feet depth. These boats could be constructed in my county, and perhaps in other parts of Canada, at a total cost, fully equipped, not exceeding $50,000. They would serve two purposes. Two guns could be mounted on them in peace time, and if England should go to war it would be Canada's duty to supply her requirements in lumber, coal and other commodities. The boats available to-day are too large to enter small ports, and we have it from officials of the Department of National Defence that in the event of a war involving Great Britain, naval raids upon Canada's Atlantic and Pacific seaboards are sure to occur. Cargoes shipped to England originate at many points and are shipped for the most part from small ports. The boats available to-day are too large to navigate in these ports, whereas boats of the type I have suggested could be used to carry cargoes from small ports. And they are quite suitable for the ocean voyage.
There are a number of captains in my county who have not sufficient funds to finance the total cost of a boat but who would be prepared to put up twenty per cent of it, and I believe that some scheme similar to the dominion housing act could be devised to arrange for financing the balance of the cost. If this were done over a period of twenty, or fifteen years, the boats could be fully paid for. The government would have an interest in them and could make arrangements to take them over in the event of war and use them for coastal defence purposes. I offer the suggestion to the minister as one which I think is sound. Not only does it offer many advantages in respect to
defence and the carrying of cargoes to England, but it would give a large amount of employment. The life of a wooden boat is about as long as that of boats built of iron or steel; the one rots, the others rust. Boats of this type can be built at a cost of about 850,000. It would be good business for the government as well as for Canada in general.
We must not forget that Canada has lost her place in transportation on the high seas, and to-day England finds herself in the same position. From my county we ship approximately 100 million feet of lumber, including pulpwood, laths, poles and sawn lumber; but I am sorry to say that ninety per cent of the primary products of my county is being transported in foreign boats. Norway is the only country that I know of to see far enough ahead that a large type of boat would not be suitable, particularly after the war. Norway built during the war, and has continued building them since, a large number of boats of suitable size which are to-day carrying to a very large extent the primary products that are going to foreign ports.
I hope the minister will give careful consideration to this suggestion. I do not mean that we should go into the building of these boats on an extensive scale, but with this large amount available I feel that some $100,000 might well be expended in order that three of these boats could be built. Arrangements could be made to have them fitted with guns in war-time, and for the training on them of naval reserves. I am satisfied that the captains I have in mind, who would have at least a twenty per cent interest in the boats, would be quite willing to cooperate with the department with a view to bringing about some reasonable understanding, thereby making some contribution to the defence of Canada.

maintopic: STATEMENT IN DEBATE ON DEFENCE ESTIMATES RESPECTING ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
In presenting this item, No. 190, the minister is asking us not only to authorize the appropriation of a sum of money but also to approve the naval policy which the item represents. The minister intimated the other day what that naval policy was. When we ask for a reason for that naval policy, the minister says he is advised to this effect by the naval officers. Surely the committee is not expected to believe that the minister accepts the advice of the naval officers without their having given good and sufficient reasons for adopting this policy as opposed to alternative policies. The minister owes it to the committee now to say why this particular policy is to be followed as against other policies. It is not enough for any minister of the crown to say he is advised by his officers that such and such is the best
Supply-National Dejence

course, without giving the reasons which those officers gave and which recommend the policy to him. There has now been considerable discussion as to courses which might be followed, and the government ought to be prepared to state what course they are prepared to follow, and why, and why it is a better or more desirable course to follow than others which have been or might be suggested. This is no time for the minister to shroud himself in silence; he ought to be stating clearly what the policy is and why he is adopting it.

maintopic: STATEMENT IN DEBATE ON DEFENCE ESTIMATES RESPECTING ROYAL MILITARY COLLEGE
speechtext:
A more elaborate explanation of the government's policy with reference to naval, air and land forces was given in the address I delivered in this house on April 26 than has ever been given before in this house. A complete definition and explanation was given of the various roles assigned to each of the three branches of the service. These were carefully thought out and, I think, expressed with sufficient clarity to be intelligible to every hon. member. In that address I endeavoured to correlate the varying functions of the three defence sendees.
In regard to policy, we are now considering the policy involved in the estimates before this committee. The functions of our naval forces were fully set out in my address of April 6. As to the question of destroyers versus submarines, the considered view of the naval staff is that for the defence of Canada destroyers are more efficient and more effective. The submarine is essentially a weapon of offence. The destroyer is effective against cruisers. My hon. friends are entitled to their opinions; I may be entitled to mine, but in regard to these questions I am relying not on my own view but on that of those better qualified to judge than either the hon. member for Weyburn or myself. My hon. friend cannot accuse the minister of not having given a complete explanation of the functions of the three defence services in Canada.
