Income War Tax Act

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
WAYS AND MEANS

speechtext:
The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Sanderson in the chair
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide:-
1.	That a taxpayer (other than a company deriving income from a metalliferous mine to which section 89 of the act applies) shall be entitled to deduct from the tax that would otherwise be payable under the act amounts not exceeding in the aggregate ten per cent of capital costs actually incurred and paid in the period beginning May 1, 1939, and ending April 30, 1940, in respect of the construction, installation, betterment, replacement or extension of plant, machinery or fixed equipment during the same period, by deducting, in each of the first three fiscal years of the taxpayer after April 30, 1940, in which the taxpayer has taxable income, an amount not exceeding one-third of the aggregate amount of the deductions authorized.
2.	That any metalliferous mine that comes into production after the 31st day of December, 1939, and prior to the 1st day of January, 1943, shall be exempt from income tax for the first three fiscal periods following the commencement of production.
3.	That dividends paid by a metalliferous mine to a Canadian company during the period that such metalliferous mine is exempt from taxation under section eighty-nine of the Act shall be exempt in the hands of such Canadian company.
4.	That the tax imposed at the source on payments by Canadian debtors to non-residents in respect of films, whether copyrighted or not, be increased to 5 per centum on the total amount of such payments.
5.	That salaries, bonuses, directors' fees, or other like remunerations, paid by Canadian companies to a non-resident, in excess of $14,000, shall not be allowed as an expense of such Canadian company.
6.	That general overhead expenses of companies shall be rateably apportioned between the taxable and the non-taxable income of such companies.
7.	That where any estate or trust is taxable under the act it shall not receive a personal exemption of one thousand dollars.
8.	That dividends paid by a personal corporation out of capital gains after all of the income of such corporation, has been taxed against and received by its shareholders shall be exempt from taxation.
9.	That the resolutions numbered 3, 5, 6, 7. and 8 shall be applicable to the incomes of 1938 and fiscal periods ending therein. Resolution numbered 4 shall be applicable on April twenty-sixth, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine. Resolutions numbered 1 and 2 shall come into force as indicated therein.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): This is the resolution to which I referred in my budget address. It provides for a tax credit with respect to certain capital expenditures during the year commencing May 1, 1939. I should emphasize

that expenditures must be of a capital nature and directed toward the earning of income in order to count for tax credit purposes. Therefore it is clear that expenditures made by a person on his own residence or for home improvement or on landscape gardening would not qualify for tax credit purposes. Expenditures which merely effect a transfer of capital will not be eligible except in the case of purchases of new machinery and equipment. Purchases of land, outlays for leases of plants or for purchases of oil or mineral properties, and expenditures on licences, patents and other intangibles will not count for tax credit purposes. In the bill which will be founded upon this resolution it is proposed to exclude residential and apartment house buildings from the operation of the tax credit. Other legislation now in effect deals with this field. It is thought desirable, for the purpose of clarification, to amend this resolution by adding the following proviso:
Provided, however, that if the amount authorized to be deducted is greater than the income tax payable by any taxpayer in any of the said three years, then the amount of such excess shall be allowed as a deduction from tax in any subsequent period in which the taxpayer is entitled to a credit under the provisions hereof, but not beyond the sixth fiscal period ending after April 30, 1940.
The effect of the proviso is this. If we assume that as a result of this tax credit measure, a completely new industry starts in 19-40 and has the experience of many new industries of not earning sufficient to make it liable for any income tax whatsoever during the first year or two, by this proviso, which I shall ask my colleague to move, the tax credit would still be available in future years, but not beyond six years from the commencement of the tax credit period. The only change from the principle of the resolution is that the proviso makes it possible to carry forward a tax credit over the years in which no taxable income is earned.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Suppose an industry over a period of three years had a taxable income but not sufficient to take credit for the amount they would be entitled to deduct; would the credit extend over to the next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: It may go forward four, five or six years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: It does not have to be specifically three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Right, but I should make it clear that the next tax credit must be

spread over three years. A man or an institution does not lose the tax credit by virtue of not being able to take his one-third, let us say, through not earning that much income.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Suppose he could take off half the first third, which would be one-sixth the first year, and next year he takes off his full third; would he be entitled to take the other one-sixth in the fourth year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Yes, not in the second and third years.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: One-sixth would, of necessity, have to go over to the fourth year.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Does the minister contemplate any amendment to the words "incurred and paid in the period beginning May 1, 1939"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: No, I was not considering changing that?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I am wondering whether
the use of these words might not discourage certain enterprises which might otherwise be undertaken. Let me point out to the minister one or two circumstances.
To deal for the moment with construction of buildings or plant, the larger the construction which is undertaken, the more fully the purpose which the minister has in mind is served. This resolution was proposed only when the budget came down in the house. Some people, we will say, are encouraged to build a $1,000,000 structure. They have to get out plans and specifications, call for tenders and award contracts. That probably will take a period of two to three months. Having done that, they have incurred liability, but payment will be made only on architects' progress estimates. It would not be possible to construct that building in nine months, having regard to climatic conditions in Canada in winter; and my thought was that so long as the obligation had been incurred, the minister would contemplate that payment for part might be made after May 1, 1940. I was going to suggest that if he hoped to have the resolution produce the effects which he had in mind he would have to make some provision in that regard, so that payment need not necessarily be made by May 1, 1940.
Another matter has been suggested to me; it was not something that came to my own mind. A firm might be encouraged by this resolution to instal a machine costing in excess of $60,000. Certain parts of it have to be imported from the United States. First those parts have to be ordered, then constructed, then imported, and then they are assembled together with other parts made in
Income War Tax Act
Canada. My information is that it would take eight or nine weeks to instal that machine in the plant, employing Canadian workmen to do it. Under the terms of purchase of the respective machines which come from the United States, the purchaser is entitled to four months' trial for satisfactory operation before being obligated to make payment. If the payment has to be by May 1, 1940, my informant tells me they will not instal the machines; but if the payment does not have to be made by then, he tells me they will. I suggest that the minister ought to give consideration to these two situations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I have had and the government has had to give a great deal of consideration to the first one; I must admit that the second is rather new.
Dealing with the first point only, the issue a? to how long we should say in this legislation that the tax-earning period shall last, I point out that a difficulty would arise with respect to any terminal date. I am thinking in terms of one very large installation which might run over the next two or three years, and which is contemplated. What I have had to say to the people concerned in such case3 is this: This is a new departure in tax credits, deliberately designed to encourage investment in capital goods and thereby create employment; I am sure that the Canadian parliament will watch with very great interest the extent to which the legislation attains these objects within the next twelve months.
Consideration can be given twelve months from now to whether or not it is desirable in the interests of the whole Canadian economy to continue for another year either this measure, some modification of it, or some other measure which experience might indicate, as being more desirable, but in the meantime those expenses incurred and paid will qualify. The concern to which the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) refers, would therefore get credit with respect to at least ten per cent of that portion of the capital expenditure which they had incurred and paid. I am afraid that any other qualification would be quite impossible of operation.
What is an "incurred" expense? On the last day of the period mentioned in this resolution a concern might incur an expense by way of entering into a contract which would not be fulfilled for a very long time. Should we thereby make it possible for them to qualify for this very generous help? I assure my hon. friend that I have given a great deal of thought to this, and I have naturally had the usual communications from industries of various kinds. In the main, I am bound to
Income War Tax Act

say, there is an apparent response from industry which is very encouraging indeed, qualified of course by those who are in the position indicated, who are contemplating large expenditures which they do not expect could be completed entirely during the period set by the resolution. My only answer to them can be that this is intended as an incentive to employment now. We do not want to put in the law anything which would make it an encouragement of employment at some time; it is an encouragement to employment now, and they can qualify to the extent that they spend money now on the objective set forth in the resolution. I do not think I can go further than that.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I can readily appreciate
the minister's view with regard to the desirability of getting an immediate expenditure. But the difficulty is, I am afraid, that if he leaves the clause as it is, he may defeat his own purpose. To come back to my illustration, if you are undertaking a million-dollar structure, the smaller part of your expense is incurred at the beginning. For example, you do not provide a tremendous amount of employment in taking out an excavation with a steam shovel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Well, that is done very quickly.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
You do not provide a
great deal of employment in the erection of the inner steel structure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Well, it is limited compared with the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: There is the making of the steel.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: That is true, when secondary industry is considered. But I am thinking of the work on the job itself, because likewise employment is provided to other secondary industries. But when you come to the laying of bricks and the doing of carpenter work, that is where your big bulk of employment comes. We can readily approve the answer which the minister said he had to give to industry; but there is the possibility, which I realize that the minister at the moment will not appreciate, that there might be an election and another government might have a very different view, and I am inclined to think that possibility may discourage some from entering upon a vast expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
There is no evidence of fear in that regard by industry.
f'Hr Dunning.]

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The trouble is that there is evidence of fear, but the fear is that business men are afraid to express it to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
They have expressed it freely to me, hence I bring it to the minister's attention. Seriously, a practical solution might reside in this. Realizing the minister's desire to create employment immediately, supposing you had words in there to the effect, " incurred and paid, and where incurred but not paid, except on progress estimates from an architect where progress is carried on with due dispatch " -or something of that kind. I realize at once that when you put in words of that kind you leave a large discretion in the hands of the commissioner of income tax. But I do not think it would be possible to leave him a wider discretion than he has under the Income War Tax Act. One of the most beneficial factors in connection with that act is that the commissioner exercises that discretion with such excellent judgment. I suggest to the minister that he is not going to get what he desires if he confines that section to the words "incurred and paid." I am pretty confident of that.
There is another aspect of the matter, on( which I think I mentioned to the minister personally. Someone has already started construction. He may be encouraged to speed it up, he may be encouraged to extend it. If you leave the words in there and they are going to be construed according to the legal meaning, you can give no benefit to such a person and hence you do not encourage him. It seems to me that you might provide a good deal of employment by simply changing the expression to " incurred or paid " instead of "incurred and paid."

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
When the minister brought down his budget and referred to this amendment, he made the statement that it was for the purpose of encouraging industrialists in this country to modernize their plants so that they could compete with industries in other countries which were selling their manufactured goods in Canada. I believe the general idea which was in his mind at the time and was left in the minds of the Canadian people was that certain industries in Canada were not as well equipped to turn out an article at a competitive price as were industries in other countries.
To my mind the biggest question in respect of this amendment is not the initial expenditure on buildings and machinery and the labour so provided, but the employment ultimately to be given in these industries

Income War Tax Act
which are modernized and given increased capacity. If that is the view of the government-and I take it that it is; I know it is my idea-then, as the hon. member for York South says, the limitation is going to affect seriously the ultimate aim of this house to provide more employment within our industries. I can well understand, for instance, that textile mills, which have to purchase their machinery chiefly in England, because we do not manufacture such machinery in Canada, would go ahead, remodel their buildings and order their machinery, and that machinery could not be delivered for six or eight or ten months and, in some instances, for a year, because at the present time it is difficult to get delivery of machinery from England. They would spend the money for these purposes, placing themselves in a position to meet competition from other countries, yet they could not claim this ten per cent under this measure because they had not spent the money. The result is they are going to hesitate; whereas if we had a long-range policy, the people of this country, generally speaking, whether heads of industry or in other capacities, having a great deal of confidence in the commissioner of income tax, would be willing to go ahead. I believe that hon. members have a great deal of confidence in the commissioner, and that, as the hon. member for York South has said, we can safely leave it to his judgment. So we could include " incurred " or take the amendment suggested by the hon. member for York South, rather than limit it as the wording stands at present.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Huron North.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
A depression results from the restriction of the consumers' income. The proposal now suggested by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is for the expansion of investments in capital goods. Are we not thereby making a back-door approach to the problem? Would it not be better to lower the sales tax and increase demand, because demand for consumer goods is the beginning of investment in capital goods. There must be a market before you want to establish a factory. If the sales tax could be removed and the sum now absorbed by that tax were used in the purchases of commodities, this would increase the demand for commodities
by the amount of the sales tax, which, as I recall it, is $126,000,000. But the national income is always substantially in excess of the total production of the nation; in fact, the national income is approximately 60 per cent above the total production. We would therefore have, if that be true, an expansion of national purchasing power to the extent of $201,000,000 from a reduction in the sales tax, which amounts to $126,000,000. I am not suggesting for a moment that it would be earned out as thoroughly as that. It is true that not all of it would be invested in consumer goods; some might even find its way into savings banks and increase investments or increase deposits in the banks. Nevertheless a determined effort to move in that direction could not fail to increase purchases of consumer goods with a consequent expansion of business in Canada. I go further. If you can secure an increased demand for goods, or an increased national income, to the extent of $201,000,000, you have practically abolished unemployment, because the additional wages or additional employment created by the production of those goods will provide labour for those who are now idle, and there would be a movement of goods into consumption. Therefore we would expand employment not only in manufacturing but in distribution.
I fancy that the answer of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) will be, quite clearly and reasonably, that we need the revenue. That is obvious; but at least a start could be made. I should like to see a little more of the experimental spirit in regard to these matters, and we can put it to the test only by making a move in that direction. And that, at best, is all that my hon. friend can do when he makes a reduction in taxation which he believes will encourage capital investment. I suggest that from a fundamental" point of view we are not making the approach which we ought to, and we are trying to establish the factory before we have attempted to provide the market, which is the essential factor, the factor which alone will bring about an expansion in demand in Canada and thereby create increased purchasing power, resulting in a reduction in the money now spent for the relief of unemployment.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS

I do not know what the minister's expectation is in this matter. I assume that when he introduced this measure in his budget, he hoped that it would stimulate industry to a large extent and in that way provide employment in Canada. But a few moments ago he spoke of the need of providing immediate employment, and I assume he has in mind the idea that this particular

Income War Tax Act

clause may provide immediate employment. It is a well known, fact, I believe, and it has been admitted in this house on many occasions, that in Canada we have the productive capacity in our industrial establishments to take care of a population much larger than we have to-day.

And we shall continue to
import goods irrespective of the tariff. If the hon. member knows the elementary facts of economics he knows that the moment you completely shut out goods from foreign countries, your export trade goes down. A reduction of imports is a two-edged weapon in our industrial life. I do not, however, wish to go into that question. Generally speaking, I believe that the present industrial establishments in Canada could take care of a much larger population, and with increased capacity they could, if the need arose, meet an almost unlimited demand. This is true of the textile industry, and it is true of a great many other industries in Canada. If I am correctly informed, the textile mills in Canada are working on short time to-day-two, three and four days a week.
If it is the intention of the minister to create employment in Canada, then I must say I do not share his optimism; but perhaps he has information which he has not so far imparted to the committee. Another aspect of the question must, I think, be considered. I cannot believe that this measure will result in an expansion in industry, because before industry can expand, there must be a market in which to sell the goods produced. Unless there is a demand for goods, no industry will go to the trouble and the expense of investing large sums on capital account. They might take advantage of this proposal and go in for replacements, and if they do so I doubt very much whether it will provide the employment for which the minister hopes. Replacements may provide very little employment ; in fact, they may do away with employment. I say that for this reason. I am informed that some of the large industrial establishments in Canada are replacing or intend to replace existing equipment with more modern machinery. They will take advantage of the proposals here made, and the

net effect will be not to provide additional employment but to reduce employment, because in the first place the machinery will have to be imported from outside, and when it is installed it will do away with the employment of a number of people who are to-day employed.
I do not know whether the minister can give us any more concrete information than he has so far given us with regard to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
It is easy for us in this house to theorize. We all do it, of course; we must, because we are acting here with respect to matters affecting the economy of the country on the basis of information which we receive from those who are directly engaged in various aspects of that economy. Naturally the evolution of the idea embodied in this resolution was not discussed with anyone prior to the bringing down of the budget. The secrecy which must prevail in such matters had to be maintained in this case. But it must be remembered that- a few years ago the national employment commission, to which reference has so often been made, gave study to this very matter, and among its recommendations was one that a great field of possible employment in Canada was represented by obsolescence rather than depreciation, and that if some encouragement were given, undoubtedly considerable employment would be opened up in dealing with obsolescence in plant and equipment which has been cumulative during the depression years.
Since the budget came down, many hundreds of communications have been received. My hon. friends have dealt with this question from the point of view of large industry only. One of the most encouraging features in the response to that item of the budget proposals has been the tremendous number of letters from those whom I call the small men, for example, the baker who has been putting up for the last seven or eight years with an oven that is not efficient in producing the kind of article he wants, or which, let us say, renders him liable to an accident. He wants to know if a new oven could qualfiy under this provision. Antiquated refrigeration plants in butcher shops and similar appliances are also the subject of correspondence. I give these only as illustrations, but it is in the multitude of these small things that employment is much more likely to be created than in a single instance of a large industry, although there are several very encouraging letters in that regard also. I cannot properly give the name, but there is one concern equipped to-day with machinery which was

Income War Tax Act
second-hand twenty-five years ago; as a result of this legislation it is even now rushing forward plans for replacing a considerable part of that machinery. When I asked, "Will that have the effect of reducing employment in the modernized plant?" the answer was definitely, "No," because modernized machinery would put them in a competitive position in fields in which they cannot now compete, and hence result in greater production.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), as I always do. I have no criticism to make of his theory, but it would be a bold Minister of Finance who would to-day propose the abolition of $120,000,000 to $130,000,000 of revenue in the belief that, filtering through in some way, some of it would come back. That has not been my experience of the abolition of the sales tax, although I have no fault to find with the hon. member's reasoning in normal times.
We have had a peculiar experience with this tax in Canada. I frankly confess that I was always concerned lest we should reach the point of diminishing returns. It is possible to get the unit of taxation so high that you defeat your objective; the law of diminishing returns commencing to operate. A curious thing in connection with this sales tax up to now has been that every increase in the unit has been followed by a more than proportionate increase in the aggregate yield of the tax. I do not say that can continue. Nothing would give me greater pleasure than to be able to present a budget here which would make possible a substantial reduction in the sales tax. It is at present one of our major revenue producers. More than 50 per cent of the national revenue comes from corporations. The measure before us at the moment is designed to encourage those people to put their money to work. I am a firm believer that idle dollars mean idle men, and in doing everything we can to encourage investment in permanent industry to overtake the obsolescence of the last ten depression years.
I admit at once that this provision is experimental, and I say to industry: I think I know the Canadian parliament well enough to believe this, that if during the year industry large and small across Canada takes hold and demonstrates that employment can be and is being created by virtue of this tax credit, the Canadian parliament, no matter what its political complexion may be at the time, will give fair consideration to the results from the point of view of extending the term of operation of this provision if national benefit continues to result. I simply ask the committee to give this provision a chance for a
year. To industry I say: Here is your chance, take hold, make this go, demonstrate that from your point of view tax credits mean an incentive; and I can trust the Canadian parliament to deal fairly with them in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house at length, but I do feel there are one or two matters I should like to mention briefly at this stage of the bill. I have mentioned on several previous occasions that I felt it was highly unfortunate that the minister and government could not see their way clear to go much farther with the plans they have already put forward. I also made it perfectly clear that I had no specific objection to the type of training being offered under the youth training plan. I did, however, make reference to the fact that there was a comparatively small number placed in jobs as a result of the training received under this plan.
Speaking on Monday May 15, the minister placed upon Hansard two sets of tables showing the progress that has been made to date. On page 4101 of Hansard it is shown that the maximum dominion contribution authorized last year was $934,382.22, which was essentially double the amount spent in the previous year.

Yes, 1937. Then if we
turn to page 4106 we find another table showing a statistical summary from the commencement of the plan in 1937 to March 31, 1939, and in group B, under the heading "Total placed in employment to March 31, 1939," we find the figure 8.029, of whom 3,282 were placed in 1937-38 and 4,747 in 1938-39. It will be noted that the amount of money spent in the second year under the youth training plan was essentially double that spent in the first year, as I have already said, but there has been only a 50 per cent increase in the number of those placed in jobs.
When the minister first introduced his youth training plan, the minister remarked that to a degree it was experimental, and that they were feeling their way. Since the introduction of that plan, he has added to the personnel of his department Mr. R. F. Thompson, who has been supervisor of the plan itself, attached to the Department of Labour. I noted with pleasure the minister's remarks concerning Mr. 
Thompson, and I need not remind hon. members of what I have already said about him. But even with the addition of Mr. Thompson to the staff, even with the experience gained in the first year under this plan, and in spite of the fact that double the amount of money was spent in the second year, I would repeat that there was only a 50 per cent increase in the number placed in jobs.
It seems to me that with the factors bearing upon the case of which I have already made mention, the results obtained might have been expected to be more satisfactory. I fully realize many of the youth training plans do not have direct employment as an objective. They are for physical training, or for some other purpose. But it is disappointing to feel that, with an authorized expenditure of a million dollars, only 4,747 jobs were obtained by those who took training under the plan.
But it is even more disappointing to look at the table the minister placed on Hansard at page 4107, and to note that in Prince Edward Island 589 were registered and took the various courses; in Nova Scotia, 1.383; in New Brunswick, 2,712; in Quebec, 17,352; in Manitoba, 5,292; in Saskatchewan, 9,848; in Alberta, 10,477; and in British Columbia, 21,893; but that in the largest province in Canada, namely Ontario, there were only 2,029, making a grand total of 71,575. So we find that only 2-8 per cent of those enrolled were residents of or came from Ontario, the most highly industrialized and largest province in the dominion. I am sure it is to be regretted that the progress of the youth training plan has been such in Ontario; for surely there are those in this province who could benefit most emphatically from training for industrial vocations of one sort or another.
All I wish to say here is that if the youth of Canada, who are unemployed and are looking for an opportunity to gain what is necessary in the way of knowledge of a craft, trade or training of one sort or another, are thus deprived of a chance to learn how to earn, there is a fundamental fault either in the scheme itself or as a result of the lack of cooperation which exists at the present time between Ontario and the federal government of Canada.
I am sure the minister will be the first to realize that the placing of about 8,000 persons on jobs, after two years of effort in connection with youth training, is actually only a beginning. I fully realize the plan the minister brings forward in this bill is to continue for three years. But if we are able to place only 5,000 a year as a result- of this training, I would suggest that the minister should look further into the plan to see if

I might point out to him what he already knows, namely, that the training itself is only part of the story, and that until from coast to coast we have set up adequate employment bureaux under federal control, to obtain uniformity and efficiency, the situation such as is disclosed in the charts recorded by the minister will prevail. We may remind ourselves that when the national employment commission brought in its report, it recommended most strongly that the existing government employment bureaux be federalized and brought under one head. maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was one who opposed the third reading of this bill the other night. I am sorry I held up proceedings, but I am not sorry I opposed third reading, because this is another thing which will create a great deal of trouble for the people of this country, particularly those in the business world. I happen to be one who was on the committee, and I see I did not scrutinize this bill as I should have done.
Section 9 reads:
(1)	The governor in council may appoint a commissioner to investigate and report on the marketing of live stock or live stock products.
(2)	For the purposes of such investigation, the commissioner shall have the powers of a commissioner appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act.
Live stock products cover a number of commodities, and this commissioner is to be given considerable power. I was mixed up in one of these inquiries one time myself, and it was not a very nice proposition. Generally speaking, whoever brings on the investigation knows nothing about the matter and no specific charges are made. As soon as a commissioner is appointed there will be an investigation, because somebody has to make some money. Hon. members will remember the investigation that was held in Vancouver into the wholesale jobbing of fruits and vegetables. Something was found wrong in that case because these people had been bringing in cars of fruit to Vancouver and then selling them in Calgary and at other points. They probably were making commissions between Calgary and Regina because they were consigning the fruit to wholesale houses of their own. An investigation was held and heavy penalties were imposed.
I am not complaining about that, but immediately afterwards an agitation was started for an investigation into the wholesale fruit trade. That was a big proposition. I believe at that time the law was that if five or six people, we will say eight people, signed a complaint to the government about any particular trade, an investigation would be held. The commissioner appointed at that time was Louis Duncan, who is well known to many of us. I have no condemnation to make of him personally, but, like any other lawyer, he was out to make the money whenever he had the opportunity.

He kept the investigation going for the three months. When his report was made there was nothing in it against any of the men in the wholesale fruit trade. The organization with which I worked for years before I went into business for myself had their books tied up for three months and it was impossible to conduct their business properly. The commissioner knew nothing about the trade, and no one connected with the investigation knew anything about it. There

was some question about proper returns not being made to the man who had consigned his goods. I remember one instance where a return was made for a certain shipment of blueberries which had been sent in by someone up in the north country. Some of those berries sold for S3 and others sold for only 75 cents, but a return was made showing the exact amount that had been received. Instead of Showing so many baskets sold for so and so, the line of least resistance was taken and only the total amount was shown. Otherwise the man would have written in to find out why one basket had been sold for $3, another for $2, another for SI and another for 75 cents. You could not convince the grower that this was due to the quality of his berries being different. Some of his pickers had picked good baskets of large berries, while others had picked small baskets covered with green stuff.
There was another instance where forty cases of strawberries had been shipped in the morning after a high market. The commission man thought the berries would bring the same price. The day before, berries had been selling for 20 cents, and he told his salesman to ask this price. A few were sold at that price to some of the earlier buyers, from the Queen's hotel at that time and from other places. Then some were sold at 18 cents, others at 16 cents, and the rest at 14 cents The average for the whole sale was 16 cents, The commission man made a return showing so many crates of berries sold at 16 cents, which was the true amount. It was not a case of stealing money or doing anything wrong. If that man had been told the different prices at which his stuff had been sold, he would have wanted to know why some had been sold at 20 and others for smaller amounts. These investigations are nonsense. They are simply a waste of public money. They are simply a means of giving a job to some fellow and give him an opportunity to make a few extra dollars for doing nothing. There is no doubt that if this commissioner is appointed there will be a job created. He will create one for himself, and put a lot of people to a lot of trouble. There is no necessity for appointing a commissioner in this particular case. I hope the minister will consider this matter and throw out this section 9. I am simply drawing attention to what may happen if this appointment is made. I am one of those who went through this bill, and I thought it was a splendid piece of legislation. The reason why business is so bad to-day is that no one has any confidence in any one.

What kind of work is

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
This vote is to cover part of the regular work of the mines branch. Laboratory and field investigations are carried on in connection with metals and minerals produced in Canada and as to the uses to which they can be put. This vote also covers the treatment of ores. In many instances, complex ores in connection with which owners of the mines have not been able to work out a process by which to segregate the minerals from the rock, are sent to the department. The ore dressing laboratory carries on experimental work of that kind, and frequently tributes have been paid to it by mining men for the assistance it has given in finding methods of treating complex ores. The vote this year, it will be noted, is the same as that of last year. Personally I know of no more valuable work carried on by the branch than the investigational work done in the treatment of ores, and but for detaining the committee I could give many illustrations of the valuable work it has done.

Supply-Mines

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I should like to corroborate what the minister has said as to the value of the work done by the ore dressing plant in this particular branch. There is no doubt that it has done excellent work.
I hesitate to delay the committee for more than a few moments, but I feel I ought to bring before it a matter which I think merits consideration. I shall make my remarks as brief as possible and ask the minister to give the matter consideration.
The ore dressing plant does excellent work and its work is, of course, experimental and advisory. If anyone has a complex ore which he wishes to have analysed, he can receive the benefit of the services of the plant, which in this way is making a real contribution to the development of the mining industry.
The particular matter to which I wish to refer is the desirability and advisability of establishing on the Pacific coast a custom smelter which would not only treat the ores that are present in large quantities, such as the copper ores of the Britannia mines, but ultimately serve as a custom smelter for the treatment of other ores from properties which do not of themselves warrant the establishment of a smelter. For the last forty years or thereabouts there has been to my knowledge a great mine within thirty miles of Vancouver which has been shipping ore or its concentrates to Tacoma on the United States side, and in recent years, to a certain degree, to European smelters. It is one of the largest mines on the continent, and I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that it has been perhaps the biggest contributor to the success of the smelter at Tacoma, which is one of the largest of its kind in the world. Yet all that we get out of this mine is the mere picking of the ore out of the ground, with perhaps a certain amount of milling and concentrating.
Canada is a big importer of metals in a refined state; we import very large quantities -I shall not give figures-of copper rods, bars, tubing, plates, wire and all sorts of manufactured or refined copper products which are used in further manufacturing processes. We are one of the big copper producers in the world, not the largest but one of the large producers, and particularly is this true of the Pacific coast. We have magnificent properties, and yet we export our copper chiefly in the form of ore or in the form of concentrates. Now that the smelter at Anyox is shut down, we do not even ship blister copper. We import metals that are double or treble the value of the ores we export, and I suggest to the minister that a
careful investigation be made into the desirability and advisability of establishing on the Pacific coast a smelter and a refinery.
I do not say that it should be a government smelter, but I think the government should bring pressure on some of the big mining companies on the coast so that a cooperative effort might be made to establish a smelter there. It would involve a large investment, and this will not be made unless there is definite leadership and considerable pressure exerted, because the easy thing for them to do to-day is simply to ship the ore to Tacoma.
The great Britannia mines-I am not criticizing that company at all because it has carried on its operations excellently-has its stock largely owned in the United States, and consequently there is a tendency, shall I say, to allow the main profit from the property to accrue to the advantage of the United States.
There is another thought which the house should keep in mind. We boast of being a great mining country, and I believe we are. In recent years the development of gold properties in Ontario and Quebec has absorbed our attention, but we are also a big producer of lead, copper, zinc, nickel and other minerals. But because we do not refine these metals here and merchandize the metal from Canada, we do not get credit in world markets of being what is known as a metal producing country. Our ore goes to the United States, where it is refined; and the United States, the western United States, in this instance, gets full credit for the merchandizing of that metal in the markets of the world. It is looked upon not as Canadian metal but as United States metal. We lose that advantage; obviously our prestige in the markets of the world as a' metal country suffers, and that is another reason why I urge consideration of this matter.
It is my desire to make my remarks very brief. There are one or two other observations I should have liked to make and I could have gone into details to demonstrate my point, but I leave the matter with the minister, simply urging that the establishment of such a smelter would be of great service and encouragement to all the smaller mining properties on the Pacific coast. From Vancouver northward to the Alaskan boundary there are scores of small mines, many of which do not warrant the installation of a smelter for the production of concentrates. But if a custom smelter were established on the coast, many of these smaller mines would be in operation to-day and could ship their product to the smelter for refining.
It is true that in the interior we have the great smelter at Trail, and the basis of that
Supply-Mines

smelter is the mine at Kimberley, which produces silver leads. I imagine that 95 per cent of the ore treated in that smelter comes from the company's own mine at Kimberley. In addition, the smelter serves many districts in the interior. But it does not serve, except at tremendous cost, many mines on the coast. There might be some rich concentrates shipped to that smelter for experimental purposes or a very small quantity for commercial treatment, but being situated 350 to 400 miles from the coast, it really does not serve the Pacific coast at all. So I would urge consideration of the establishment of a smelter on the coast, not necessarily by the government, but through its leadership.
