speechtext: Give leadership.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Well, "giving leadership"
is a very broad term.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Surely it is. It gives
plenty of scope for action.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: And if I might add, it is a very much over-worked term.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
But I am thinking of
real leadership.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I agree as to the value of a smelter on the Pacific coast. Certainly the mines department would be willing to give all reasonable encouragement short of digging into the public treasury. I do not see that we could go very much further than that. May I observe that the condition to which my hon. friend refers applies only to the Pacific coast. Canada is a producer of base metals in very large quantities. We 
have the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company's plant at Trail, producing mainly zinc and lead.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Silver.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Silver also, but I am speaking now of the base or commercial metals. This mine produces and refines both lead and zinc in marketable shape. Another large base metal producer is the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company's plant at Flin Flon, Manitoba.	They also produce
zinc of very high quality, I think I may say the highest-quality zinc produced in north America, probably in the world. Coming to copper, we have a large copper production at Flin Flon, because the mine I have mentioned is a copper and zinc mine. There is also a very large production of copper at Sudbury and at Noranda. Those are our three main producing copper mines, outside the Britannia mine in British Columbia to which my hon. friend referred. There are refining plants for copper at both Sudbury and Montreal, and in those plants copper is carried to the final point of processing for use in wires or rods or any other form which commerce requires. As regards nickel, Canada is the largest producer in the world, and there is a large nickel refinery at Port Colborne. Therefore the business of carrying our base or commercial metals through to the point where they are usable is very well established throughout Canada with the exception of the Pacific coast.
As to what might be done at the Paciric coast, I can give my hon. friend the assurance now that any persuasive power I have, and I am sure, any persuasive power the government has, would be gladly exercised towards getting a smelter established on the coast. I would, however, make this observation, that if there were the assurance of supplies of these concentrates on the Pacific coast for many years ahead, probably capital might be attracted to the building of a smelter. Beyond that, I would not want to commit myself at the present time.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: It must be borne in mind that for the last thirty-five or forty years the Britannia mine has been shipping its ore or concentrates to Tacoma or Europe, and that mine alone would sustain a smelter. There is no question as to the quantity of supply.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Well, the question which naturally arises in one's mind is why those

Supply-M ines
associated with the Britannia mine have not completed the process by erecting a smelter and completing the treatment of their products.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: That is very easy to understand, and in this I am not particularly critical of the management. The mine is owned very largely in the United States; it is a great American concern, and naturally the owners favour the treatment of the ore at Tacoma. That is the answer, so far as I can see; and that is the reason I suggest that the government might call in the officials of the company and talk seriously and earnestly to them about the matter, with a view to inducing them to establish a smelter in this country. I can imagine some form of pressure which I do not wish to discuss here. There is a way in which the government could put a little pressure on the company and get it to see the light, as it were.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I understood the hon. member for Kootenay East to say that some of this ore was shipped to Europe and then returned here. Could he explain, or could the minister explain to the committee, how it comes about that it is cheaper to ship the ore to Europe and pay duty on the finished product returned to us, when the finished product could be made in this country?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I did not say, "shipped to Europe"; I said that they did in recent years ship to Europe, but over a period of thirty or forty years they shipped the ore to Tacoma, where it was smelted and refined. I also said that Canada during all this time has imported very large quantities of copper products.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: But if they shipped the ore to Tacoma they would still have to pay duty on the finished product coming from the United States into Canada; and I should like to know how they could afford to ship to Tacoma, when there are in this country smelters which can produce finished goods? How can they ship ore to another country, paying freight to Tacoma, ship back the finished product to Canada, paying the freight on the return journey and the duty as well, and still sell as cheaply as can be done in this country?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: It is probably only within the last four or five years or certainly within the last ten years that copper refining plants have been established in Canada. The same is true in a measure of zinc. The mine in northern Manitoba which I mentioned a moment ago as a producer of zinc has been in operation for only seven or eight years.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: They have been producing copper for some years at Trail. Is there not a refinery in process of construction at Trail?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: They have a refinery.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Imports of refined copper
have gone down steadily, because we are now in a position to refine our own copper and produce our own requirements. I would expect this to continue and that our imports of refined copper from other countries will soon disappear entirely, because we are doing this work ourselves. The same is true of zinc, lead and nickel. The only place to which- it is not a criticism-the observations of the hon. member for Kootenay East would apply, is on the Pacific coast.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
In 1915, I brought this
question to the attention of the house, and the Prime Minister of that day, Sir Robert Borden, asked me to take it up with Colonel Carnegie, who was associated with the munitions board. This I did. Colonel Carnegie went to British Columbia and looked over the field, and a copper refinery was established. But it was established at Trail. I had wanted it established on the Pacific coast. Colonel Carnegie, however, investigated the interior situation, and a refinery was established at Trail for the refining of copper. For some years they refined copper and produced rods and bars. But the mine at Princeton, the Granby mine, closed down; copper prices fell, and Trail then ceased to operate the refinery. Some of the machinery and equipment may be there still, but they have not carried on the refining of copper at Trail for some time. That, however, is not the point. The point is that Trail cannot serve the Pacific coast, which is 450 miles away, and that is where the heavy production of copper ores takes place. That is where the smelter and refining operations should be located. There was one at Anyox which was based upon the production of low grade copper ore from the property at Alice Arm, but that was closed down. It was operated for something like twenty years, but that is at the extreme northerly end of the province, 500 miles away from the Britannia mines to which I have referred.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I wish to support the
hon. member for Kootenay East in his request. I do not know of anything that would be of greater benefit to British Columbia than a smelter and refinery. Along the tide-waters of British Columbia there are a large number of small mines which could be reached, and the product could be taken to a smelter where
Supply-Mines

coal mines are operating. The result would be of considerable benefit not only to the larger mines but to the smaller ones as well. I do not know in what way the government could give assistance; for I for one would not encourage them to go into business; they are, in my opinion, already sufficiently in business. Some encouragement should, however, be given to the establishment of a smelter on the Pacific coast, especially seeing that we have coal mines there ready to assist in the work.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I have no objection to the
erection of a smelter on the Pacific coast; in fact, I should be glad if arrangements could be made and an industry established there. At the present time, however, the Britannia mines must be shipping ore somewhere for conversion into copper, and I am wondering whether it is shipped out of the country. Can the minister or the hon. member for Kootenay East inform the committee whether that copper ore is exported and brought back into Canada as a finished product?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Once the ore goes out,
its identity is lost and it enters into the general operations of the smelter at Tacoma, or the one at Swansea, or wherever it is sent. I did not wish to labour this question beyond bringing it to the attention of the minister, but the point is this. If we established a smelter and carried on refining operations at the coast, Canada would get the benefit of the labour operations that enter into the production of the refined metal, and that is the most valuable part of the labour.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: But there is the other point to be considered, whether Canada could find an export market for the finished product.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: To what extent is assistance given to prospectors or small operators under this or any other item? What is the policy of the department in granting assistance?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The department gives no assistance to prospectors apart from the information supplied through geological surveys, mapping and related work.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Here is $424,000 spent on inquiries and so on. Who is getting the benefit of this-the government, or some person who has a mine of some kind? It is well to be frank, because the business world is not getting very much of a show in expenditures of this kind. I have many stocks that do not look honest to me, and if the government is spending money for investiga-[Mr. Mayhew.}
tional work I think they should look into the activities of concerns, with high-salaried executives, in which people have money that is stolen away.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The benefits that accrue from the work carried on under this vote might be described as indirect. Let me give an illustration. The Flin Flon mine in northern Manitoba, which I mention because I am familiar with the facts, was discovered some twenty or more years ago. It was ascertained, after a few years of exploratory work, that there was there a very large body of ore, copper, zinc and gold, with some silver; but it was found that the ore was difficult to treat. It is what is known as complex ore. Quite obviously, if a mine were to be established there, some method of treatment of the ore would have to be found, and I am well within the mark when I say that considerable assistance was given by the ore-dressing .laboratory in Ottawa. They carried on investigational work for months, and as a result partly of their contribution a method was devised of treating this particular ore. What was the result? In northern Manitoba an important industry was established which, before it turned a wheel, had invested, in milling plant, buildings, machinery, water power development and hydro line, over $30,000,000. To-day this industry gives profitable employment to some 1,700 workers. In that community a town with more than 7,000 inhabitants has been established, and it is known that the mine has a long life ahead of it yet. The point I am making is that the department of the mines branch that carries on the work under this particular vote was able to make a useful contribution-*

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: -to the establishment of this particular mine.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Who owns the mine?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The shareholders.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Who are they?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The shareholders, I understand, are mainly in the United States and Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Chiefly United States capital, I believe.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Possibly, but a substantial amount in Canada. It was United States capital that initiated the enterprise; I know of no good reason why United States capital should not come into Canada and develop our resources.

Supply-Mines

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
It is simply this,
that a number of people come into Canada, make an investment and get the benefit of this expenditure made by the government. It is United States investors who draw the dividends for the life of the mine, which is considerable. I sometimes wonder how far the government is justified in making this great contribution to those who come in and reap the proceeds.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: My hon. friend, when he makes that statement, is showing only a small part of the picture. The fact is that this mine pays corporation taxes not only to the federal government but to the provincial government on its net earnings, a very substantial contribution. In the second place a considerable number of its employees earning salaries pay income tax both to the province of Manitoba and to the federal government and so add to the public revenue of the country-

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: And that is only one property out of scores that benefit under this vote.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Quite so. Third, we have the sales tax. A considerable amount of the $2,750,000 more or less that is paid in wages at the Flin Flon mine contributes to the public revenue through the sales tax. In addition, a market has been established there for a great deal of agricultural produce from other parts of Manitoba, because even radishes or lettuce cannot be grown on muskeg or barren rock. The hon. member's statement carries an implication that is not warranted. It is quite true that United States capital came in to develop this property. To my personal knowledge over a million dollars was spent in exploratory work before the option was taken up by the people in New York who held it. I know whereof I speak when I say that there was grave doubt in the minds of investors from the United States whether they had not made a mistake in putting their money into this property. But I say that if capital comes from the United States, develops a property like this, pays taxes including income tax, and builds up a community which provides a market for many of our products- and we certainly need markets in the prairies for all kinds of agricultural products-it is a good and healthy thing for Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I agree to a large extent with what the minister has said. I believe the government are doing useful work in carrying on these investigations or surveys of our natural resources; it is an important part of the functions of government. But I doubt
whether the government go far enough. After spending much time and money on certain useful social services-that is really what it means, as the minister pointed out, the social value of opening up these mines-they have not gone far enough. One thing that is clear is that when you take a certain amount of ore out of a mine there is that much less ore left in the mine. Some day that mine will be exhausted. In various parts of Canada, particularly British Columbia, we have a number of ghost towns that at one time were prosperous mining communities. Millions of dollars, possibly billions, were taken out of those mines. When the best part of the ore was taken out, the mines were abandoned, and the community that had gathered there were left to shift for themselves.
I believe the time has arrived in Canada when the government should take a greater interest in mining in various parts of Canada. I think the minister said they have ascertained that at Flin Flon there is mineral for a number of years to come. I believe that a certain amount of the profits made in these mines should be set aside as a fund to remove the people who work in that community to some other economic field of endeavour when the mine is exhausted.
When I was in Sweden a few years ago, a somewhat similar project was brought to my attention. A gold mine was opened up within the arctic circle; the capital was provided partly by the government and partly by private interests. A model town was built, and every year a certain part of the profit from the mine is set aside so that when the mine is exhausted the community built up round it can be moved to some other economic area, and the people will not be left stranded and become a charge on the state as in this country when private interests have finished operating a mine and abandon it. Such a provision would be a good thing not only for the people concerned but for the government. I would commend that idea to the minister in connection with this commendable work which is being done in surveying and research to get the greatest social value possible out of the resources of Canada.

Item agreed to.
Bureau of geology and topography.
12S. Bureau of geology and topography administration and miscellaneous services, $144,000.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
This item and the two or three immediately following ones cover the geological and topographical surveys. I do not notice any great increases in these items, and I think they should be increased. In parts
Supply-M ines-Geology

of Alberta and Saskatchewan in the last two or three years a considerable amount of oil has been discovered. In the Turner valley there is now a tremendous production. I commend the government for the work done in these different oil fields; they have discovered and given valuable information to those drilling for oil and gas in western Canada. But my criticism is that now we know that under a substantial area of that country there is oil and gas, we should be sending out more parties for topographical and geographical survey work there.
There is the Delbonita field; then to the north is the Blood Indian reserve field. North of that are the Pekisko hills, and then Turner valley. Then there are Moose Mountain and Two Pines. Just south of Calgary a new structure known as Twin Domes has been found lately. Then north of Moose Mountain are Jumping Pound, Greece Creek and Hunter Valley. Just the other day another field came in about one hundred and thirty miles east of Calgary showing a different class of oil, altogether, one we have been endeavouring to find in western Canada. I refer to an asphalt base oil brought in at Steeseville. Last January a new well came in near Lloydminster, on the boundary between Saskatchewan and Alberta.
This means that first of all there must be topographical survey work done by a party, and that must be followed by geologists. As I understand the situation, in the past two or three years we have had only two parties doing geological work and only two or three topographical parties. It has been determined that there is -a strip of land from the United States boundary, about twenty miles in width, running right through the Liard river, about eight hundred miles north, which is all first-class prospecting country for both oil and gas. If considerable work were done by the department, there is no doubt more structures would be developed there, and a great deal more oil produced in Canada.
I hope the minister has in a supplementary item appropriations sufficient to put more parties in the field. If not, I hope he will take the matter into consideration in another year, and see that we have a considerable increase in both the topographical and geological survey parties, so that this useful work may be carried on for the good of Canada.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I should like to say a word of commendation to the minister for the work done under this item, and of course I would express the hope that he would do still more. In the district I represent is to

be found the Zeballos area which is probably the richest in all Canada-and I am not sure if it could not be said it is the richest
on the north American continent. I do not think in all Canada there is another area of comparative size in which the same rapid progress and development have been made. There are certainly three and very soon there will be four mills shipping gold constantly. The first one which came in ships something like $150,000 worth of gold every month. That is the shipment, not of a year but of a month. There are two other mills shipping, and another one to be brought in. Inside two years a town of 2,000 people has grown up.
Geological surveyors from the department now under consideration were sent out there in the last four or five years. At first they gave only casual reports on conditions. It was, I suppose, desirable that the government should be cautious, and they did not go too far. But the reports they made were such as to draw the attention of prospectors to the area. Unfortunately, the British Columbia mining branch got off on the wrong foot. Their reports condemned this area, which rather gave it a black-eye. But the reports of the dominion government were always favourable, and those reports have been more than amply justified. It was somewhat due to the reports they got out, the surveys they made and so on, that further exploration took place. It is a hard country to prospect because of the wooded conditions in it and also the steep and rugged mountains.
The people in that area are extremely anxious to have further geological surveys made in- order to extend the field. Of course grounds are staked all round, and further information is wanted. I inquired this year if a geological party were to be sent out, and I was told it was impossible to send one until a further topographical survey had been made. I understand there is a party now on the ground, and I hope that will lead to a geological survey next year.
I am not criticizing or complaining, but I am pointing out that this is a fabulously rich area. We do not hear much about it, but stuff that gives 72 ounces of gold to the ton, at the present price of gold, speaks for itself. It is not one isolated claim. There are scores of them which seem to yield about the same proportion, and an enormous new development will take place in the neighbourhood. The government would be well advised to spend money on these surveys. They say, "Oh, it costs money to do that." But when one mine ships $150,000 worth of gold every month, it shows how well repaid any efforts

Supply-M ines-Geology
by the government would be. I hope the department will enlarge the sphere of its operations at that point because there is ample scope and ample prospect of success.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) has said. I believe the minister would be well advised to spend a little more money in topographical and geological surveys in northern Saskatchewan. The well at Lloyd-minster brought into production last year is plenty of evidence of the oil in the northern part of the province. I should like to impress upon the minister the importance of carrying on this work. Would the minister state how many survey parties will go out this year, particularly in the northern area?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
In respect of what the hon. members for Qu'Appelle and Moose Jaw have said, undoubtedly there is a considerable weight to the point of view they express. The discovery of crude oil in large quantities in the Turner valley within the last three years has stimulated exploration for oil in the western provinces. A year ago we had two parties of oil geologists operating. This year we shall have four parties in the field. Those four parties will operate in Alberta.
One of the difficulties experienced by the department is that of getting the necessary personnel to head the parties studying oil formations in the prairie provinces. It is a comparatively new thing in this country. The matter is under constant study, and the policy of the department is and should continue to be an extension of this service, so far as oil is concerned. I repeat, however, that it is necessary to obtain the services of experienced personnel to head geological parties.
In addition to the four parties studying oil structures, we shall have several topographical parties doing mapping work, and collating the related information so as to enable a better study to be made with respect to oil structures in Saskatchewan and Alberta. It is now known from superficial examination that there is probably a very considerable number of oil structures in each of these provinces. The information given by the hon. member for Moose Jaw in connection with recent discoveries in Alberta bears out that statement. I would say that the prospects for the discovery of large fields of crude oil in western Canada are certainly encouraging. I think I am within the mark when I say that in its present dimensions the Turner valley field is the largest crude oil field in the whole British empire by a considerable margin. Of course when one examines the possibilities of this field he must consider the possibility of obtaining markets. This is being studied at the present time by the Alberta government. If markets are to be found, ordinary methods of transporting crude oil will have to be developed. When we consider that this field is only of comparatively recent origin, we must admit that considerable progress has been made. I have no doubt that the resourcefulness of those associated in the development of this field, together with the sympathetic interest of the Alberta, Saskatchewan and federal governments, will make substantial progress in this direction before a great period of time has lapsed.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to say that four geologists were going out to Alberta this summer?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Four parties.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
A great development
is proceeding in the northwest part of Saskatchewan where an abundance of gas has been discovered at Lloydminster. Last fall there was a considerable crude oil development about twelve miles west of Unity by the Unity Valley Oil Company. I understand that six contracts have been let for development work this spring. I do not want the minister to overlook this territory, because we expect it to outclass even the Turner Valley in the not far distant future.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
The question of funds is
perhaps not an important matter at the moment, although it is important in the final analysis. The main difficulty is in getting experienced personnel to head the geological parties, especially those carrying on oil examinations. That is something which, before very long, will be overcome. So far as Saskatchewan is concerned, I am advised that reconnaissance work is being carried on by the department. This is in the form of general examination of structures to gain a lead as to where geological examinations might be more intensively carried on. I think we should keep in mind that this development is only of comparatively recent origin. It is about in the same position to-day as our general mineral development was twenty years ago.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
This is a vote that I want to support. Geological surveys and other similar work by the mines branch seem to me well worth while. I am referring not only to this government but to all governments in the past. We must not forget that had it not been for our tremendous mineral pro-
Supply-Mines-Geology

duction during the past few years it is doubtful if we would have been able to pay our external debt. The total vote for the mines branch is $4,949,000, which includes an item of $3,500,000 for subsidies on coal. This leaves about $1,500,000 to be spent on the mines and geology branch. According to the Canadian Almanac, the 1935 mining production was valued at $429,000,000. I believe I am right when I say there is no other department of the government that spends so little for such a huge production. I do not mean to suggest that this department is wholly responsible for this tremendous production, but it has played its part in research work, geographical and topographical surveys and so forth.
A moment ago the minister referred to the Turner valley oil fields. This field may well become one of the great discoveries of Canada. As long as I can remember we have been hunting oil in this country, but we never found any large quantity until the Turner valley field was opened up. Not long ago an English capitalist whom I know was in this country. He told me he had gone out to Turner valley with Bob Brown of Calgary and his son, and had decided to put into one development $81,000 of his own money. He spoke most optimistically of the chances of a pipe line being constructed from the Turner valley to the coast. If that field develops as we hope it will, there is no doubt that a pipe line will have to be built to the coast, and possibly another one to the prairies or to the head of the lakes. The British government would be quite happy co have supplies of oil on the Pacific coast, and the United States government perhaps would appreciate having extra supplies there. The question of research was mentioned a few moments ago. The item covering this particular work has been passed, but it is only by research that we can hope to make any advance, whether in mining, manufacturing, agriculture or any other industry. As the matter was being discussed, I thought of the International Nickel Company. I cannot give the exact date, but I do not think it is far back of the beginning of this century when these great nickel deposits were lying idle. Yet to-day we produce 90 per cent of the nickel of the world. It was only by research that a method was discovered to utilize this nickel. Because of this research we have to-day one of the great developments of Canada. I have heard members of this house refer to the fact that Americans put money into this country and are taking out large dividends. As the minister pointed out, while some dividends do go out of

Canada, United States money has been risked. Huge sums are paid out in wages and for the purchase of supplies. I have forgotten the exact figure, but I believe about 80 per cent of the value of production remains in Canada despite all the dividends that are paid. This money is paid out in wages, salaries, and the purchase of supplies in this country. The fact that United States money comes into Canada to develop the country is only to the good so far as we are concerned. It only means that whoever discovered the property was unable to get Canadians to gamble on its development. I rose merely to say that in a general way I think we should give every encouragement to our mineral development.
I quite agree that the exhaustion of a mine leads to a ghost town such as the hon. member spoke of, but that cannot be helped; for as you clean out the property, the town cannot carry on. I think every encouragement within reason should be given to the mining industry of Canada to continue to produce. The only industry that surpasses it in production is agriculture, which includes wheat growing and all other branches. Forestry, for example, is $100,000,000 below mining production for 1935. On fisheries we spent $2,000,000 more than we spent on mining, if you leave out the coal subsidies, and in 1935 it produced $35,000,000 of products, or about 10 per cent of our mining production. I wanted to say a few words on behalf of the mining industry, which is such a great asset to the section of the country from whence I come, as well as to northern Ontario, Manitoba, Quebec, British Columbia and some other parts of Canada. I believe this house can do nothing better, generally speaking, than to encourage the expenditure of reasonable amounts of money on different branches of research and geological surveys to encourage the production of mineral wealth from the bowels of the earth.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Moose Jaw suggested that the government make more intensive surveys of the oil structures in Alberta with a view to increasing our oil supply. While I am in favour of that, I would point out that our oil production has already increased to such an extent that we are unable now to find a market for it, and the efforts of the government should be directed more towards the development of markets than to further production, unless the government is prepared to extend pipe line facilities to the oil producers of Alberta. I would ask the minister how much money has been spent in the last three years, compared

Supply-M ines-Geology
with what is to be spent this year on surveys of the oil areas of Alberta.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: It is difficult to carry and have available at a moment's notice all the details of expenditure on every one of these items. I have not the information before me, but I can have it supplied to the hon. member if that is satisfactory.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The minister can perhaps let me have it later. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that encouragement should be given to Canadian industry and to the investment of Canadian capital in Canadian industry. I know that foreign capital investment in this dominion benefits us to a certain extent, but too much foreign capital invested in a country is not to its best interests. I believe that plenty of capital is available in Canada and that we should give every encouragement to Canadian capital to develop the production of goods from Canadian resources. The government have stated that they are anxious to do something for the oil industry in Alberta. Just what assistance has the federal government given to the oil industry of Alberta during the last three or four years? Have they done anything to assist the oil industry in extending markets, and, if so, just what steps have been taken in that direction?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: So far as extending markets is concerned, to use the expression of the hon. member, the department has not entered that field. Its work has been confined to gathering all available data concerning the geology of Alberta so far as the means at its disposal would permit, and in gathering information regarding the geology of other parts of the country, which information later on has led to mining development. That, together with proper mapping and making the data available, has constituted in the past the work of the department in this respect, and it has not gone beyond that to find markets. That has been left to private enterprise, and private enterprise up to the present has been on the whole pretty successful in achieving that objective.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I do not think the
government has assisted the oil industry of Alberta to as great an extent as it could have done. I believe that more could be done if there were proper cooperation between the federal government, the department of lands and mines of Alberta, and the oil industry.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: In what way, for instance?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
In dealing with the
importation of oil from Montana and other
foreign oil-producing fields. Surely steps can be taken to make available to the oil producers of Alberta, markets in the adjoining provinces, if not the servicing of British ships on the Pacific coast, and extending a pipe line as far east as the great lakes, so that Alberta oil can be made available to consumers in eastern Canada. Would the minister indicate the degree of cooperation there has been between the federal government and the department of mines and resources of Alberta. Has there been any cooperation?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The hon. member asked what amount of money had been spent in Alberta in the last year. Only a few field parties were out there, and $17,500 was spent on these parties last year. But the hon. member must remember that the natural resources belong to the provinces, and for any work the dominion government do in that direction they should be commended. They have made available to us perhaps the best geologist on the north American continent, and he has done exceedingly valuable work. His work has been followed by those who have had money to invest in drilling wells and endeavouring to find oil. His work has been carried to the point where there is enough known about the Turner valley to-day to enable a pipe line to be put through to the coast. Credit for that should go to this dominion government and former dominion governments for supplying the men they had in the field doing that work. The reason why I spoke in the first place was that with the tremendous oil area there is, with its possibilities of oil and gas, if we continued with just the few parties we have had up to date it would take from thirty-five to forty years to cover the territory, and I was glad to hear the minister say that more parties will be put in the field. The dominion government and the federal Department of Mines and Resources deserve every credit for what they have done. They have shown the way and have done most valuable work in connection with Turner valley and other fields, in order that money might be invested and further discoveries made. As a matter of fact, the work of the geologists has been so good that they have been able to call within a few feet where oil might be found six or seven thousand feet below ground. All this work was done by the dominion government.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
No, you are wrong
a mile.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
All the exploratory work was done by the dominion government. Alberta and Saskatchewan have done
Supply-Mines-Geology

very little, although they are doing what they can. But they have not men of the calibre of the officials the dominion government has in that field; nor can they get them; and I believe we should give all credit to the minister and his department for what they have done.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Let us hear you name the men.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Doctor Hume.
There is no better geologist in this or any other country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Let us hear some more.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Under the agreement the natural resources revenues belong to the province. I understand that the minister was at the last meeting of the council of mining and metallurgy. Has he received any requests with reference to this item, the bureau of geology and topography, from the mining departments of the universities or from the national council of mining and metallurgy?
The government of Canada is spending a great deal of money on roads and on other agencies, and providing health service and tax relief benefits for the mines of this country. It appears in the minister's own annual report, page 10, that the receipts of the bureau of geology were only $8,465.75; and the total expenditures during the year for the purposes of that bureau are shown at $850,269.94. In the large universities of Canada at the present time, owing to the rapid development of our mines, there is a great increase in the number of students of mining. They go through the course of training in the fall and in the spring; and in the summer months it should be the function and the duty of the department to utilize the services of these students to develop the natural resources of the country, in relation not only to geology but to all branches of mining. That is what Germany has been doing for the last twenty years. In this respect we are marking time and standing still. I have read the reports for the past ten years. Here are a few lines from the last one:
The value of production from Canadian mines in 1937 reached a new record of $457,359,092, an increase of 26 per cent over the previous peak year, 1936. This production was made up as follows: metals, $334,165,243, an increase of 29 per cent, fuels, $65,828,879, an increase of 9-7 per cent, other non-metallics, $22,495,271, an increase of 34 per cent, and clay products and structural materials $34,869,699, an increase of 34 per cent.
In the light of these developments the minister will agree, I think, that students in our universities are selecting the right course. 
Their preference used to be for electrical and mechanical engineering and other departments of science, but now mining is at the top. Has the minister received any recommendation from the council of mining and metallurgy favouring a national forward policy of development in view of what could be done in the mining industry for the people of Canada? I think the department has a duty in this regard. I know that those who go to the department from the universities find it hard to get anything done for them in the summer time. It seems to me that, instead of these appointments being handed over for distribution by the professors in charge of these universities to their bright students, they are handed out on the recommendation of government members. I do not care to say that this statement is wholly correct, but I have found it to be so on three or four occasions in my own experience. I do not say that the department is idle; far from it, it has made a great deal of progress; but I plead with the minister, as I have pleaded for the past ten years, that we should take a leaf out of the book of Germany, go to work and develop the natural resources of this country. Reference has been made to twenty-six metals and to the progress which has been made in mining. It seems to me that the department is too top-heavy in the city of Ottawa. Look at the details of this item on page 103 of the estimates; it is nearly all headquarters-brigadier generals, generals, ordinary captains, lieutenant-colonels and all these dignitaries at the top of the department, leaving the privates in the field to go out and make surveys, develop the country and find out what is going on, with their salaries making up a comparatively small part of the item.
I have been reading the annual report of the university of Toronto, which is one of the leaders in this particular department of science. Some of their brightest students are in the mining school of the university. Before the war Germany utilized in practical work all of its students; so did the Czechs. The result was that their countries became among the most highly industrialized in the world, whereas we are spending in this branch of the administration only $144,000, a thousand dollars less than last year. The same tendency is to be noted year after year; we sit here and pass this item, and I can see no forward policy to deal with what might be done from coast to coast to develop the activities of the department and utilize the services of these capable students. The mining school of the university of Toronto is, I believe, the largest in the history of the university. There are chances for these young men if they will go

Supply-M ines-Geology
out and do hard work throughout the country, and they are doing it every year. Some of the members of the varsity football team are now going north to get some practical experience in the mines; and if the department would employ also some of the high school students in the summer, it would be doing a good service. In Germany they take care, in the branches I have named, not only of university students but of high school students, and in that way they have contributed to make their country one of the world's great industrial states. I think the minister should inform us if he has received suggestions along this line,, and what is being done about it.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I do not want to
detract from any credit which is due to the federal government for what they have done for the development of the oil industry in Alberta. But may I point out that it was not until October, 1930, that the province gained administrative control over its natural resources. It was in 1914 that the first oil developments took place in Alberta.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Not oil.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Well, speculation in oil. There was great gambling in oil leases, oil shares and that sort of thing-possibly some of them were sold as far away as Vancouver-and I conclude that this was the only thing which developed from whatever contribution the federal government made to the oil industry in Alberta. We cannot give this government credit for developing Alberta's oil industry, because all the development which has taken place there has been since the natural resources were turned over to the province. How the hon. member for Moose Jaw can claim credit for this government for the development of the oil industry, I do not know. Its development has now proceeded to such an extent that we have sufficient proof of the oil structure: something should be done in the way of extending the markets rather than in making more extensive surveys. I should like to know from the minister what cooperation has been given by his department to the department of lands and mines of Alberta in the development of the oil industry-

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I shall endeavour first to answer the hon. member for Calgary East; then I shall address a few remarks to the hon. member for Broadview.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Do not waste any
time on him.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary East has rather an active imagination this evening.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: We have plenty of evidence of that.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: He criticized the Department of Mines and Resources for not doing something, or for not doing more, about finding markets. Practically everything that has been done in the study of oil structures in Alberta has been done by the federal government-either this or preceding administrations. It is true the university of Alberta has on its staff a gentleman who has given a good deal of study, although, I believe, more or less incidental study, to oil structures in that province, and with quite useful results, but the main work has been done by the federal department. I would point out further that we get no revenues federally from the production of oil in Alberta apart from the revenue we may receive indirectly from corporation profits tax, or sales tax and the like.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Or income tax.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Or the tariff.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
The royalties on the oil go to the province, and properly so. I suggest, therefore, that some responsibility rests upon the province of Alberta for finding markets. We are cooperating in every reasonable way we can. At present, as is generally known, there is a small delegation in Great Britain taking up the matter of interesting British capital in the furthering of development. They have in mind the possibility of a pipe line to Vancouver, which was referred to by the leader of the opposition. We have given every assistance we can in supplying data and information. More than that, at the request of the minister of lands and mines of Alberta, the Hon. Mr. Tanner, we sent over to that delegation, at our own expense, Doctor Hume, who has been studying oil structures in the Turner valley, so that there would be available to the delegation any technical information which he might be able to supply with regard to the geology of the area and its possibilities.
The hon. gentleman apparently lays the whole responsibility on the federal government for finding markets. In this contention he is really going a little too far. If we controlled the resources and obtained the royalties on production, we might perhaps in a way be fairly criticized along the line of the hon. gentleman's observations to-night; but I
Supply-M ines-Geology

am confident that the industry itself, if it gets the sympathetic support of governments-I do not necessarily mean financial support-will be able to solve the problem of markets within a comparatively few years. After all, I repeat what I stated a short time ago. This development has taken place only within the last few years. If any one had said five years ago that there was a potential field in the Turner valley capable of producing several hundred million barrels of crude oil, he would probably have been laughed at.
The additional information that has been made available through drilling and the study of the structure as revealed in the cores that come from the drilling, has enlarged the area of the available data, so that experienced oil geologists, the best on the American continent, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw has said, have been able with a good deal of certainty to estimate the potential production of the Turner valley. This has happened only in the last year, as a matter of fact. This information is all available. It was not available two years ago, and on the basis of this information I have no doubt that capital can be interested to develop the pipe lines, which appear to be one of the chief necessities in getting this product on the market.
So far as the hon. member for Broadview is concerned, he has not been fully alive to what _ is being done in the department. He criticizes the department because it does not employ university students. As a matter of fact the parties that are sent out by the federal Department of Mines and Resources to do geological work in the field are composed mainly of university students, who are taking courses in mining engineering and geology, and I think I am within the mark when I say that this very year about 150 students from the universities of Canada will find places on these field parties. Why are we doing this? We wish to give all the encouragement we can to the young men in our universities who are specializing in geology or in mining and engineering. It is worth something to young men who are taking these courses to have the opportunity of going into the field under experienced chiefs of parties and doing the actual field work under their direction.
Let me say to my hon. friend that his suggestion is not a new one. It has been followed by the department for a number of years, and it is producing results that are useful not only to the department but, as well, to those students who are getting practical experience in the work that they
[Mr. Crerar.3
have chosen for their future careers. I should like to see more money spent in enlarging our fund of information on the geology of Canada. After all, Canada is a vast country. We do know enough now, however, to be certain of the fact that over immense areas we may reasonably expect to find not only precious minerals but base or commercial minerals as well; and while the hon. gentleman criticizes the expenditure at headquarters, as he puts it, and points to the revenue that is obtained, I would suggest to him, what I suggested to the hon. member for Winnipeg North, that while we do not get results directly in dollars and cents from this expenditure, we do indirectly benefit greatly. For instance, gold production in Canada has increased greatly. In 1935 it was about 8118,000,000; the next year, over $131,000,000; the next year, over $143,000,000.
In 1938 the total gold production in Canada was $168,000,000; and I venture the prediction to-night that in 1939 it will probably be $185,000,000. What does that mean? It means that all these companies engaged in all this development, are making their contributions to the national revenue through the taxes levied on their profits, and through the sales tax not only on the large amount of materials and supplies that they require but through the wages paid to their employees. In addition, many individuals are paying income tax to the federal and provincial governments as a result of this development. In these ways, while we do not directly get dollars back for the expenditures we are voting here to-night, we get them back indirectly. I doubt if there is anything today that has fertilized public revenue in this country more effectively than the mining development that has taken place from one end of Canada to the other. I am sure that the vote we are discussing is a very necessary expenditure if that development is going to continue.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I did say that the department is doing good work. Could the minister give the division of the two hundred students among the universities?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: I have not that information here, but I can tell my hon. friend that those students are certified by the civil service commission on the reports received.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Who selects the students?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Students in the third and fourth years in mining engineering and

Royal Visit
geology are eligible to come into these parties. They apply, and the civil service commission rates them on the standing given by the professors in the universities. That method is working out very well. It is an incentive to the students in their student work because they realize the value of the practical knowledge that they gain through the field work. I should like to see it enlarged.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: The minister was kind enough to nod his approval when I was speaking about the Zeballos area, but that does not show in Hansard. Would he mind saying a few words of encouragement to us, as to his intentions in going on with the work?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: Being a minister charged with ministerial responsibility, I might hesitate to be quite as enthusiastic as my hon. friend about the Zeballos area, but I can say that to-day it is one of the most promising areas in Canada. An old mine manager with many years' experience said to me a few years ago that it takes several years to make a mine. He said: "You may get your surface showings, and they may go down a few hundred feet, but I want to know what is down 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, 5,000 feet." So far as our information goes, this is a promising area, and if its present prospects hold I may say to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni I do not think he has over-stated its possibilities; but I would hesitate to predict just what the future of this area may be, because we have not yet the complete evidence of the depth to which gold bearing veins go. But the information we have points to the correctness of the statement made by the hon. member.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
May I point out to the hon. member for Moose Jaw that there was no development of the Turner valley oil field or of any oil structure in Alberta while control of the natural resources was in the hands of the federal administration. There was, as I pointed out, a little gambling in oil leases and shares, but no real development of the oil structures prior to the return of the resources to the province. May I also point out that the greatest development has taken place since the province has been blessed with a Social Credit government. In giving the federal government credit for the Alberta oil developments, the hon. member for Moose Jaw surprises me, particularly after the minister telling us that because the federal government secures no direct revenue from the oil produced in Alberta he feels no concern about marketing that oil, which, he says, is a purely provincial matter. I would remind the hon. member as well as the minister that
in 1935 we heard a great deal about marketing. The Liberals not only were going to reform the monetary system but were going to extend Canadian markets.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: And we have.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext: But the development of markets for Alberta oil is as important to western Canada as the development of markets for the products of eastern Canada, and the fact that the federal government does not receive any direct revenue from the oil production is no reason why this government should not do everything in its power to extend the markets for Alberta oil.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
I understand there is some arrangement to close to-night at ten o'clock. I therefore move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT WITH RESPECT TO OFFICIAL PROGRAM FOR SATURDAY, MAY 20

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ROYAL VISIT
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT WITH RESPECT TO OFFICIAL PROGRAM FOR SATURDAY, MAY 20
speechtext:
I have been asked to give information to members of the house about the arrangements for Saturday. Inquiries have been made as to the facilities for members of parliament to get from the ceremony of the trooping of the colour to the site of the supreme court building for the ceremony there. It has been learned from the acting commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that members of parliament who are in the reserved enclosures on the driveway near the centre gate will have no difficulty in proceeding, after the departure of His Majesty and of the Prime Minister, through the centre gate and west along Wellington street to the supreme court building.
However, it will not be possible to arrange any special facilities for members who prefer to witness the trooping of the colour from the windows of the centre block. The police
The Royal Assent

anticipate such large crowds that the task of making any special passage through the crowd would be an insuperable additional burden to their ordinary police duties. Members of parliament are therefore urged, if they desire to be present at both ceremonies, to make use of the reserved enclosures near the centre gate for the purpose of viewing the trooping of the colour. Then they will have no difficulty in proceeding to the supreme court building.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East), the house adjourned at 10.04 p.m., until Friday, May 19, at 2.30 p.m.
